Poisoned Vultures in the Kruger

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Over 400 vultures and many lion, leopard have been poisoned in the Kruger in the past two years, what's happening and why isn't this public knowledge?

Unique Selling Point:
We got a call from several sources within the area telling us that there had been mass poisonings - mostly of birds of prey - like vultures, bataleurs etc the biggest being over 100 vultures, 10 lions and 2 leopard just in one poisoning earlier this year. This has been devastating for the populations of vultures, as they are highly endangered - we cannot even afford to lose one says EWT's Dr Lindy Thompson. She says that there has been an increase in these instances for two main reasons, one for using body parts in muthi markets (esp in west africa) and two because they are the first sign in the sky that a kill has been made, and poachers are trying to get rid of them as not to alert the anti-poaching units. EWT has all the data and incidences cataloged which is very helpful!

Summary:
We are going to meet with Maholoholo's brian jones, who has collected evidence and data over the past few years, he is worried that there is something more sinister, all of the poisoned animals go to him on contract from the kruger. We are also speaking to the former head of the kruger Dr Solomon Joubert who is bitterly upset about the poisoned animals - he believes that the Kruger needs to do more to protect our heritage and that they are not making it public as they should.

Further information:
So the plan and cost is below:

Drive up Wednesday 4th nov morning:
CAP car - so only fuel cost on petrol card (R2,000) - I spoke with Nikola and this is possible to use it from wed-friday. I just need to tell vince.

Arrive in Hoedspruit 1ish
meet with lindy and john (couple) from endangered wildlife trust - case studies/experts - go through the information, and get everything from then 2-5pm

Thursday - drive an hour to Maholoholo - case study 2/expert- meet and go through all the information with Brian Jones - who has all the pictures, video's evidence of vultures being poisoned and the knowledge.
then on that basis he says he'll give me an interview on how to rehab the birds, so we will see actual birds from the Kruger that were brought in now. poor things. so that will take the day.

Confrontation: I'll have asked the Kruger for an interview for Thursday afternoon or Friday afternoon in Hoedspruit - or Monday in Pretoria (it's up to them).

Friday morning - go with the EWT and go ring vultures and see how it affects them
do their interviews and get all that done... and then go back home after (or do interview with kruger as per above)

Monday (only presenter day)
Interview main case study brian jones
Links with derek - potentially we do them in a bushy area... and with the visuals of all the dead ones...
Confront with kruger (if then)

So in terms of crew:

ONLY ONE presenter day
Two nights stay in hoedpsruit for myself (air Bnb) like last time R1500 or R3000 if there's a camera man in terms of stay.

Cameraman - so it would be me and cameraman with sound etc - Xander Foster R5,000 for thursday/friday

And then another camera man in johannesburg. The reason I'm shooting 3 days isn't because I want to but it's the only way to get around over such an expansive area, and we are saving costs in other ways.




Extra Budget Items:
I can finalize this in the morning but this would be my estimate.

Cameraman 3 days: R5,000 = R15,000
Presenter 1 day
Edit - 3 days: R3,600 = R10,800
R2,000 for travel - petrol card - so i don't need the cash...
R190 X3 - sasha away, R200 for cameraman lunch and R300 for monday = R1070
So yeah i think that's 10 minutes, unless something else Phenomenal happens lol

Also there are no EDITORS AVAILALBE lol so i can only have floris from 23rd nov (which is fine), if I shoot this and another one back to back and edit that week to finish both stories in time for AM. Up to you

Script:


Majestic birds of prey - like the vulture - can spot a meal from the sky from kilometers away and are often the first to arrive at a fresh kill made by a carnivore.
Lindy: They're so entertaining. You get the little shy guys around the edge and then you get the ones like rugby players that just muscle in there.
But that circling flight which signifies a carcass may be one reason why hundreds are being poisoned in the Greater Kruger area. Ecologist Dr Lindy Thompson is project coordinator for vulture conservation and research at the Endangered Wildlife Trust or EWT.
Lindy: It's like being at a funeral. It's really awful. And there's an awful smell as well, like acrid chemical smell that stays with you for a few days.
THE SPATE OF POISONINGS HAS STEADILY INCREASED KILLING OVER 500 VULTURES OVER THE PAST TWO YEARS ALONE… AND ROSE FURTHER DURING LOCKDOWN LEAVING LION, LEOPARD, HYENA – EVEN OMNIVORES LIKE THE DUIKER – IN ITS WAKE. ANY ANIMAL THAT INGESTS THE POISONED WATER OR MEAT, WITHOUT HELP, WILL SUFFER A CRUEL DEATH.
Lindy: So birds that generally have this shaking like uncontrolled muscle spasms when they die, they often lie face down with the wings out, these poisons, one of them is called two-step because the bird it eats and then it literally takes two steps and then it dies.
Thompson’s husband, John Davies, also works under EWT’s Birds of Prey program.
John: if we're losing 20, 30 birds at each poisoning scene and almost all the birds are critically endangered or endangered even two to three large poisonings a year could theoretically be enough to functionally wipe out the vulture population.
Lindy: If there's any surviving animals, living vultures or other animals like hyenas or jackals that might still be alive, you need to deal with them and get them away to a place of safety, a rehab center or a vet.
Manager of rehabilitation centre Maholoholo Brian Jones has rescued animals from poisoning crime scenes for 60 years.
Brian Jones: A pride of lion dead, a leopard dead, a lioness dead with fifty four and six leopard face vultures did well poisoned. We saved two out of six, 5 tawny eagles poisoned. We saved one. When you see that, it breaks my heart.
Jones’ team is equipped to deal with many different species of carnivores and raptors.
Brian Jones: I've got to get I've got a first aid kit. I get my two girls who I've trained… they went straight away like we went to punda maria 50 for vultures point and two lion cubs and a leopard poisoned all dead. The moment they get there they give them atropine and incubate them with a tube and flush flush the kidneys out, every hour and half.
This is their latest poisoned victim - a 40 year old white backed vulture… Jone: “It’s about 3 years he’s been here now,you can he’s not well at all, I don’t know if he’s going to make it.”
Sadly he didn’t. Once all the surviving animals are rescued, the carcasses left are burned to avoid further secondary poisoning.
AS THE GREATER KRUGER AREA IS SO VAST, ROUGHLY THE SIZE OF ISRAEL, IT'S DIFFICULT TO ACCURATELY CALCULATE HOW MANY ANIMALS DIE FROM POISONINGS AS OFFICIALS CAN ONLY COUNT THE KNOWN INCIDENCES, MEANING SOME ARE LIKELY NEVER PICKED UP OR PICKED UP TOO LATE TO AVOID SECONDARY POISONINGS - WHERE AN ANIMAL EATS A POISONED ANIMAL AND BECOMES POISONED THEMSELVES, LEAVING EXPERTS TO SUSPECT THAT THE NUMBERS WE HAVE MAY ONLY BE THE TIP OF THE ICEBERG.
Dr g: we found that their were seventy one incidents in the last 10 years or so and that about two thousand animals have died.
During her 16 years as a Veterinarian at the Kruger Dr Danny Govender has specialised in disease ecology which looks at pathogens between humans and animals in a shared environment.
Dr g: What happens when you have small pieces of meat that get them strewn all over the environment, You don't have a concentration of animals dying, we don't really know what is being missed. Between the snaring and the poisoning, especially in the north western side of the park, it's starting to impact lion populations to the level where there isn't really functional prides anymore.
There are several hypotheses as to why these poisonings are happening: poaching for the pot, muthi for traditional healers who believe vultures help them tell the future and purposeful poaching where a waterhole or meat is poisoned.
John: One of the most significant is what we call sentinel poisoning, where people are actually trying to deliberately poison birds, because vultures give away the location of poached carcasses: if you get rid of them, you have a better chance of not being arrested or not being found. Also in some ways accidental poisoning without actually targeting other species, somebody might be targeting lions or hyenas.
Solly: We have a legal obligation to look after the biodiversity of our national parks.
Dr Solly (saloman) Joubert has 55 years of experience in wildlife management, he began at the Kruger as a section ranger and worked his way up to become its director in the early 90’s.
D: Many theories as to what's behind these poisonings. What do you believe?
Joubert: It's a part of the whole rhino syndicates that are driving this for income, it is just greed.
VULTURES AND OTHER BIRDS ARE INCREDIBLY IMPORTANT TO THE ECOLOGY OF OUR REMAINING WILD AREAS, AS THEY ARE KNOWN AS THE “CLEAN UP” CREW – SCAVENGERS WHO EAT DECAYING MEAT – WHICH OTHERWISE WOULD SPREAD DISEASE.
The fear is that if we lose them, we could have more zoonotic diseases which can cross from animals to humans.
Thompson: This is what happened in India. There was an example in the 1990s where there were three species of vultures declined by over 90 percent in just a few years, and they had huge disease increases with huge health care costs to the people of India.
Dr g: That was a catastrophe, the world responded, this is not just a wildlife crime, this is a human crime. So there's two groups of poisons mostly implicated organo-phosphates and the other major group is the carbonates.
These are widely used in agricultural food production for pesticides and insecticides.
Dr g: you should really be be a responsible consumer. You should be asking what chemicals were used and am I happy with that? when society is aware, they will also put pressure on all different sort of organs of state to actually do their job
Do you think the government has been slow to react?
Yes, I think they have that. And that is my one criticism about this. this is not good news, you know, and the public has a right to know. They don't have the right to every detail. There's a lot of detail that can be sensitive, but at least you tell people that there is something going on. And we are looking at that.
Dr g: the awareness needs to be broader. I completely agree. And so we're actually running an awareness campaign about the impacts of poisons, we need to make sure that all sort of law enforcement monitoring, all of those organs of state and different government departments need to come together to make this happen. And that takes time.
So the Kruger has partnered with EWT’s manager for the vultures of africa program Andre Botha to implement a vigorous training program with park rangers to identify poisoning crime scenes.
Botha: over a period of about 10 weeks we were able to train all of the field rangers identify a poisoning incident and then secure that scene while protecting himself and then raising an alarm to get a response out to that scene.
Dr Govender says they’re looking at tightening the legislation around the possession of poisons and have formed a poison task team with government to deal with agricultural pesticides.
If you actually found in a protected area with poison, it doesn't matter if you don't have a little or a permit from the thought managing authority to possess those poisons. It should be sentences.So who's monitoring these things? So everybody who's selling. Those poison registers need to be checked.
The EWT and Kruger conducted a vulture population survey which will be released next year. As the birds migrate across African borders its best practice to concentrate on their local nesting grounds.
Botha: if you consider that of those 500 birds, probably 50-60 % were breeding adults that were killed theres no doubt that it will have an impact on the population overall.
Its 7am in a park near the Kruger and the couple are trying to catch vultures in order to fit them with GPS tracking devices that will keep tabs on the birds movements.
John: And these send data through every five minutes of a location throughout the day. And it'll give us paint a better picture about what areas are they relying on? Where are areas of concern, which from our perspective is poisoning is a big deal, understanding if they're going into areas that we know are a bit of a hotspot for poisoning. And also, if we have any of our transmitters stop moving, it's an immediate reason to go and investigate because it does happen that sometimes attract birds actually do sort of indicate where there is a poisoning scene or a bird has died.
(Action scene) Two white backed vultures were captured – Gandolph and Braveheart - who were carefully tagged and then released back into the wild. Within a day, Gandalph was sighted in the Kruger.
WHAT SOME SOUTH AFRICAN’S MAY NOT KNOW IS THAT THESE ANIMALS BELONG TO EVERYONE – AS THEY ARE PART OF OUR HERITAGE - WHICH IS WHY IT’S SO IMPORTANT TO COME UP WITH A SOLUTION TO THE POISONING CONUNDRUM BEFORE ITS AFFECTS ARE IRREVERSIBLE.
Brian Jones: habitat loss
Despite the loss of our wild areas, there may still be hope for our 7 local vulture species.
S: I think it it's time that we all stand up together and say, man, this this is our heritage. We want our heritage and we're going to do our part to build it up again.
Thompson: Imagine going on a safari and not seeing vultures. They're just there and we take them for granted and it would be a big loss, I think, to our natural heritage if we don't have that anymore.

Dr g: That was a catastrophe, the world responded, this is not just a wildlife crime, this is a human crime. So there's two groups of poisons mostly implicated organo-phosphates and the other major group is the carbonates. These are widely used in agricultural food production for pesticides and insecticides. Dr g: you should really be be a responsible consumer. You should be asking what chemicals were used and am I happy with that? when society is aware, they will also put pressure on all different sort of organs of state to actually do their job Do you think the government has been slow to react? Yes, I think they have that. And that is my one criticism about this. this is not good news, you know, and the public has a right to know. They don't have the right to every detail. There's a lot of detail that can be sensitive, but at least you tell people that there is something going on. And we are looking at that. Dr g: the awareness needs to be broader. I completely agree. And so we're actually running an awareness campaign about the impacts of poisons, we need to make sure that all sort of law enforcement monitoring, all of those organs of state and different government departments need to come together to make this happen. And that takes time. So the Kruger has partnered with EWT’s manager for the vultures of africa program Andre Botha to implement a vigorous training program with park rangers to identify poisoning crime scenes. Botha: over a period of about 10 weeks we were able to train all of the field rangers identify a poisoning incident and then secure that scene while protecting himself and then raising an alarm to get a response out to that scene. Dr Govender says they’re looking at tightening the legislation around the possession of poisons and have formed a poison task team with government to deal with agricultural pesticides. If you actually found in a protected area with poison, it doesn't matter if you don't have a little or a permit from the thought managing authority to possess those poisons. It should be sentences.So who's monitoring these things? So everybody who's selling. Those poison registers need to be checked. The EWT and Kruger conducted a vulture population survey which will be released next year. As the birds migrate across African borders its best practice to concentrate on their local nesting grounds. Botha: if you consider that of those 500 birds, probably 50-60 % were breeding adults that were killed theres no doubt that it will have an impact on the population overall. Its 7am in a park near the Kruger and the couple are trying to catch vultures in order to fit them with GPS tracking devices that will keep tabs on the birds movements. John: And these send data through every five minutes of a location throughout the day. And it'll give us paint a better picture about what areas are they relying on? Where are areas of concern, which from our perspective is poisoning is a big deal, understanding if they're going into areas that we know are a bit of a hotspot for poisoning. And also, if we have any of our transmitters stop moving, it's an immediate reason to go and investigate because it does happen that sometimes attract birds actually do sort of indicate where there is a poisoning scene or a bird has died. (Action scene) Two white backed vultures were captured – Gandolph and Braveheart - who were carefully tagged and then released back into the wild. Within a day, Gandalph was sighted in the Kruger. WHAT SOME SOUTH AFRICAN’S MAY NOT KNOW IS THAT THESE ANIMALS BELONG TO EVERYONE – AS THEY ARE PART OF OUR HERITAGE - WHICH IS WHY IT’S SO IMPORTANT TO COME UP WITH A SOLUTION TO THE POISONING CONUNDRUM BEFORE ITS AFFECTS ARE IRREVERSIBLE. Brian Jones: habitat loss Despite the loss of our wild areas, there may still be hope for our 7 local vulture species. S: I think it it's time that we all stand up together and say, man, this this is our heritage. We want our heritage and we're going to do our part to build it up again. Thompson: Imagine going on a safari and not seeing vultures. They're just there and we take them for granted and it would be a big loss, I think, to our natural heritage if we don't have that anymore.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Over 400 vultures and many lion, leopard have been poisoned in the Kruger in the past two years, what's happening and why isn't this public knowledge?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We got a call from several sources within the area telling us that there had been mass poisonings - mostly of birds of prey - like vultures, bataleurs etc the biggest being over 100 vultures, 10 lions and 2 leopard just in one poisoning earlier this year. This has been devastating for the populations of vultures, as they are highly endangered - we cannot even afford to lose one says EWT's Dr Lindy Thompson. She says that there has been an increase in these instances for two main reasons, one for using body parts in muthi markets (esp in west africa) and two because they are the first sign in the sky that a kill has been made, and poachers are trying to get rid of them as not to alert the anti-poaching units. EWT has all the data and incidences cataloged which is very helpful!
metadata.Summary: We are going to meet with Maholoholo's brian jones, who has collected evidence and data over the past few years, he is worried that there is something more sinister, all of the poisoned animals go to him on contract from the kruger. We are also speaking to the former head of the kruger Dr Solomon Joubert who is bitterly upset about the poisoned animals - he believes that the Kruger needs to do more to protect our heritage and that they are not making it public as they should.
